title: Procurement / legal - usage definition redlines (ZenChat)
summary: ZenChat procurement/legal walked through redlines focused on (1) defining usage units (tokens/requests/embeddings), (2) retry/fallback behavior and double-charging concerns, (3) caching and whether cache hits are billed, (4) audit logs and retention/access controls for usage data, (5) invoice dispute window and process, and (6) credits/true-ups and how/when credits apply. Redwood agreed to send updated clause language options (token definition + retries + caching), a short billing/metering FAQ, and a proposed dispute window compromise tied to invoice preview + usage exports. ZenChat asked for evidence of audit logging and clarity on whether they can export daily usage in their preferred timezone.
topics: Definition of “Token” and alignment across OpenAI-compatible endpoints
What counts as a billable request (streaming, tool calls, partial completions)
Retries, fallback routing, idempotency, and avoiding double counting
Caching / cache-hit attribution and billed vs raw tokens
Usage data retention, audit trails, and access controls
Invoice preview, dispute window length, and late-arriving usage events
Credits: issuance, expiration, application order, and rev-rec constraints
next_steps: Redwood (Sofia) to send revised usage-definition clause options (token definition, retries, caching, dispute) by 2026-02-13
Redwood (Nadia) to share a one-pager on billed_tokens vs raw_tokens + cache_hit attribution and how it shows up in usage exports
ZenChat (Mark/Priya) to confirm preferred dispute window (30/45/60 days) and whether they need a separate “invoice preview” step in the process
ZenChat (Samir) to send their internal audit logging / retention requirements (minimum retention, who can access, evidence format)
Schedule follow-up redline working session after ZenChat reviews updated language (target week of 2026-02-17)
action_items: Sofia Mendes: Provide redline language for token counting, retries, caching, and dispute window (due 2026-02-13)
Nadia Rahman: Provide metering semantics write-up for streaming/tool calls/retries + idempotency note (due 2026-02-14)
Jordan Blake: Send invoice preview + usage export workflow proposal (due 2026-02-14)
Priya Desai: Confirm commercial preference for credits (expiry, cap, and applicability) and share procurement template language (due 2026-02-18)
Samir Khan: Provide ZenChat security requirements for billing logs retention/audit access (due 2026-02-18)
questions: How exactly is a “token” defined for chat vs completions vs tool calls, and is it consistent with OpenAI-compatible endpoints?
If Redwood retries a request server-side (or falls back to another region/model), do we get charged twice?
Are cache hits billed? If partially served from cache, how does that show up on the invoice/exports?
Can we get an immutable usage export we can reconcile, and what’s the audit trail if numbers change (late events/backfills)?
What’s the dispute window, and can we receive an invoice preview before the invoice is finalized?
How do credits apply (order of operations vs overage), and do credits expire?
transcript:
Meeting: Procurement / legal - usage definition redlines (ZenChat)
Date: 2026-02-11
Time: 4:00pm - 4:52pm PT
Duration: 52 min

Attendees
- Jordan Blake (Redwood) 
- Sofia Mendes (Redwood)
- Nadia Rahman (Redwood)
- Priya Desai (ZenChat, Procurement)
- Mark Liu (ZenChat, Legal)
- Samir Khan (ZenChat, Security)
- Elena Petrova (ZenChat, Finance Ops)

---

[00:00] Jordan Blake: Alright, I think we’re recording. Thanks everyone for making time. Goal today is to go through the usage definition redlines and make sure we’re aligned on what’s billed, what’s not, audit logs, dispute process, credits. Sofia and Nadia are here with me.

[00:18] Priya Desai: Yep, thanks Jordan. We want to keep this pretty scoped. Our procurement template is strict on usage based services.

[00:27] Mark Liu: And we’ve got some specific language around “usage units” and “measurement,” and I want to make sure it’s not ambiguous.

[00:35] Jordan Blake: Totally fair.

[00:36] Sofia Mendes: Hi everyone. I’ll jump in on legal clause options, and Nadia can cover the technical metering semantics.

[00:44] Nadia Rahman: Hey.

[00:47] Samir Khan: Hi.

[00:48] Elena Petrova: Hello.

[00:52] Jordan Blake: Cool. Mark, do you want to start with the top redline you’re most concerned about?

[01:00] Mark Liu: Sure. The definition of “Token.” Right now your draft says something like “token as measured by Redwood systems,” which is basically “trust us.” We need a more objective definition. Also you’re offering an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, right?

[01:17] Jordan Blake: Yes, we have OpenAI-compatible APIs.

[01:19] Mark Liu: So we want it aligned to that behavior. Otherwise engineering will compare numbers and we’ll get into disputes.

[01:28] Nadia Rahman: Yep. So, practically, tokenization depends on model family. For the OpenAI-compatible endpoints we have aligned counting semantics so that prompt tokens + completion tokens match what the client expects from that interface. Internally we store raw tokens and billed tokens. The billed tokens are the canonical for invoicing.

[01:48] Mark Liu: “Billed tokens” is not in the agreement though. That’s what I mean.

[01:52] Sofia Mendes: Understood. We can make it explicit. A common approach is: (a) define the unit as “billed tokens” as reported in the usage API/export, and (b) specify that the usage report is the source of truth, subject to a dispute window and correction process.

[02:12] Priya Desai: We’re open to “usage export is source of truth” if there are guardrails and audit trail. Our issue is: if you change the meter, how do we know?

[02:23] Jordan Blake: Makes sense.

[02:24] Nadia Rahman: On meter changes: we do change control. We can provide notice for material changes and we keep versioning internally. Also we’ve been adding shadow-billing comparisons before changes hit invoices.

[02:37] Samir Khan: Can you log those changes? Like auditable records that on date X you changed token counting?

[02:44] Sofia Mendes: We can commit to maintaining an audit trail for material meter changes, and to providing notice in advance when practicable. The exact phrasing we can propose.

[02:56] Mark Liu: Let me be concrete. Our redline says: “Token means a unit of text as defined by the applicable model tokenizer, and the number of tokens will be the number reported in the usage records made available to Customer.” Something like that.

[03:12] Nadia Rahman: That’s reasonable. Only nuance: tool calls and structured outputs—some tokens are in the tool call arguments. But they are still part of model input/output tokenization.

[03:23] Mark Liu: Fine, as long as it’s counted consistently.

[03:27] Jordan Blake: Yeah.

[03:28] Elena Petrova: From Finance side: we need ability to reconcile. We usually do a daily export and compare to internal spend.

[03:37] Jordan Blake: We can provide daily usage exports. There’s also a usage API.

[03:42] Elena Petrova: We saw in one of the calls you mentioned timezone issues in exports? We need it in UTC, or at least consistent.

[03:51] Nadia Rahman: We can do UTC. If you want a local timezone view, we can discuss. But for reconciliation, we recommend UTC.

[03:59] Priya Desai: Okay.

[04:01] Mark Liu: Next item: retries. Your terms say you may “retry requests to maintain reliability.” We can’t be charged twice if your system retries.

[04:13] Jordan Blake: Agreed. We don’t want that either.

[04:15] Nadia Rahman: So there are two categories: client retries and server-side retries. For server-side, we use idempotency keys and dedupe at the usage event level, so the same request shouldn’t double bill. There were some historical edge cases—streaming disconnects, fallback routing—where the meter could double count, but we’ve been hardening that.

[04:38] Mark Liu: This is exactly why we need language. If it happens, do we get a credit automatically or do we have to discover it?

[04:45] Sofia Mendes: We can add language that “Customer will not be charged for duplicative requests caused solely by Redwood’s internal retries” and that if billed in error, we will correct via credit or invoice adjustment in the next billing cycle.

[05:02] Priya Desai: “In the next billing cycle” is okay, but we want a timeline.

[05:07] Sofia Mendes: We can propose “within one invoice cycle after verification” or “within 30 days.” We’ll draft options.

[05:15] Samir Khan: How do you prove it wasn’t our client? Like, we need logs.

[05:19] Nadia Rahman: Our usage events include request_id and idempotency_key when provided. For OpenAI-compatible we support idempotency. If your client uses it, it’s easier to attribute. Also we can show duplicate detection metrics.

[05:35] Mark Liu: We can add idempotency keys. But the agreement shouldn’t require us to do extra work to avoid you double billing.

[05:43] Jordan Blake: Totally. Idempotency helps both sides, but it’s not a condition.

[05:48] Priya Desai: Good.

[05:50] Mark Liu: Next: caching. Your redline response says you might use caching. If you cache and serve from cache, are you charging us for tokens that didn’t run on GPUs?

[06:04] Jordan Blake: The policy depends on the product and the customer config, but generally we bill based on billed tokens, not GPU seconds, for Hosted API.

[06:13] Mark Liu: That didn’t answer the question.

[06:15] Nadia Rahman: Sorry—let me. For Hosted API, caching can reduce cost and latency. We track cache_hit attribution. Today, default behavior is: if a response is served from cache, billed tokens may be reduced depending on the cache type. For prefix cache, there’s still model compute for new tokens. For full response cache, you can configure whether it’s billed or not. Most customers want “don’t charge for full cache hits.”

[06:43] Elena Petrova: You said “may be reduced depending.” That’s risky.

[06:47] Nadia Rahman: Right. That’s why we expose fields: raw_tokens and billed_tokens, and cache_hit flags, so you can see it per request aggregated. And contract language can say “billed tokens are as reported.”

[07:03] Mark Liu: We need it more deterministic. Can you commit: cache hits are not billed?

[07:10] Jordan Blake: We can commit for specific caching modes, but I don’t want to accidentally commit to something that breaks the product when it’s not a full cache hit.

[07:19] Sofia Mendes: We can structure it as: (a) define caching categories, (b) state billing treatment for each. For example: “Full response cache hits: not billed. Partial/prefix caching: billed for tokens generated plus any non-cached prompt tokens as reported.”

[07:39] Mark Liu: That’s closer. We’ll need to review the exact definitions. We can’t have “as reported” do all the work.

[07:47] Priya Desai: And also, if Redwood turns on caching without telling us, our reconciliation changes.

[07:52] Jordan Blake: Understood. For enterprise, we can agree caching config is transparent and controlled—either in the console or via contract exhibit. Nadia?

[08:02] Nadia Rahman: Yeah, it can be pinned at the deployment config level. We can document it.

[08:08] Samir Khan: Also, do you store prompts for caching? That’s a data concern.

[08:13] Nadia Rahman: Caching can store prefixes or responses. It’s encrypted at rest in our infra; retention is configurable. For some customers we disable caching. We can also scope caching to non-sensitive routes.

[08:27] Samir Khan: We’ll need that in the security annex, but okay.

[08:30] Mark Liu: Next: audit logs. Your security FAQ says you have “audit logging,” but the agreement says nothing. Our requirement: access to billing/usage data must be logged, and logs must be retained for at least 12 months.

[08:46] Sofia Mendes: We can include an obligation to maintain audit logs for administrative access to customer usage/billing systems and to make them available upon request subject to security constraints. Retention: we can propose 12 months, possibly longer depending on plan.

[09:05] Jordan Blake: We generally have audit logs. We’ll confirm exact retention.

[09:09] Samir Khan: “Make them available upon request” — we want at least a report or evidence packet. We don’t need raw logs if that’s sensitive.

[09:18] Sofia Mendes: That’s reasonable. We can say “provide reasonable evidence of audit logging on request,” or “audit log exports for a scoped time range.”

[09:30] Elena Petrova: And access control: who internally can see our usage data?

[09:34] Nadia Rahman: Restricted. Finance and certain engineering on-call roles, with access approvals and audit logging. We’re tightening that further with access controls on billing tables.

[09:48] Priya Desai: We’ll want it documented.

[09:51] Jordan Blake: We have an internal policy, and we can share the customer-facing version.

[09:56] Mark Liu: Next: dispute window. Your standard says 30 days after invoice. We need 60, ideally 90. Usage-based billing takes time to reconcile.

[10:10] Jordan Blake: We can look at 60.

[10:12] Sofia Mendes: The challenge is rev-rec and close process; we also have late-arriving events and we need finality. But we can propose a process that gives you an invoice preview window, plus 45 or 60 days dispute period after invoice issuance.

[10:29] Mark Liu: What do you mean by “late-arriving events”?

[10:32] Nadia Rahman: Sometimes events arrive late due to pipeline delays. We aim for near real-time but there can be a lag. Also backfills if we discover a missing dimension. We try to avoid retroactive changes, and when we do, it’s controlled.

[10:49] Mark Liu: I don’t want a surprise adjustment two months later.

[10:53] Sofia Mendes: We can add language limiting retroactive corrections absent fraud or mutual agreement, and stating that corrections primarily apply prospectively.

[11:06] Priya Desai: That helps.

[11:07] Elena Petrova: Could we get an “invoice preview” like 3 business days before invoice goes out? Then our team can reconcile.

[11:16] Jordan Blake: Yes, we can implement an invoice preview step for enterprise.

[11:20] Sofia Mendes: If we do that, could you accept a shorter dispute window? Like preview + 45 days.

[11:27] Mark Liu: Possibly. I need to see exact language.

[11:31] Samir Khan: From security angle, I also want the logs for the preview export—same access controls.

[11:38] Nadia Rahman: That’s consistent.

[11:40] Jordan Blake: Okay.

[11:41] Mark Liu: Credits. Your MSA says credits are “discretionary.” That’s a no-go. If there’s a billing error, we need a defined remedy.

[11:51] Sofia Mendes: Agree. We separate two things: (1) service credits for SLA issues, (2) billing corrections for erroneous charges. We can make billing corrections non-discretionary: if verified, Redwood will issue a credit or refund per agreed timeline.

[12:10] Priya Desai: Also promotional credits: we need to specify expiration, and whether credits apply before discounts or after.

[12:19] Jordan Blake: For commercial credits, typically they expire 12 months unless otherwise stated, and they apply to usage charges before payment is due—like a prepaid balance.

[12:30] Elena Petrova: But how do they show on invoice? We had an issue with another vendor where credits were applied a month late.

[12:37] Jordan Blake: We can commit to showing credits as a line item on the invoice and in usage reports.

[12:43] Nadia Rahman: Technically, credits apply at billing ledger time, not at metering time. So you’ll see gross usage, then credits applied.

[12:54] Mark Liu: We want the agreement to say credits apply automatically and are not at your sole discretion.

[13:01] Sofia Mendes: For negotiated credits, yes. We’ll draft: “Credits issued under an Order Form will be applied automatically to applicable fees until exhausted or expired.” For dispute corrections, we’ll draft a remedy clause.

[13:19] Priya Desai: Okay.

[13:20] Mark Liu: Another point—definition of “request.” Your pricing is per token, but you also mention request limits and quotas. Does a failed request count?

[13:31] Nadia Rahman: Good question. We meter requests primarily for rate limiting and analytics. For billing, we generally bill tokens. For failed requests: if it fails before the model runs, tokens are zero. If it generates partial output then times out, it may have billed tokens for the portion generated, but we can treat certain failures as not billable depending on status code and cause.

[13:53] Mark Liu: That sounds messy.

[13:55] Jordan Blake: The goal is fairness. If you got output, there’s some value; if it’s our fault, we can credit.

[14:02] Mark Liu: We need a clean rule. Like “only successful responses are billed.”

[14:09] Nadia Rahman: Streaming complicates “success.” Sometimes the client disconnects after receiving most of the content. Also tool calls can return partial. A binary rule can be gamed.

[14:20] Priya Desai: We’re not trying to game it. We’re trying to avoid surprise.

[14:24] Sofia Mendes: Perhaps we define “billable usage” as tokens generated and transmitted to Customer, excluding duplicative tokens due to Redwood error, and excluding tokens from requests that return a Redwood error prior to any token transmission. And then for disputes, we have process.

[14:44] Mark Liu: Better. But I want to make sure “transmitted” is measurable.

[14:48] Nadia Rahman: We can reference what’s recorded in usage events. For streaming, we record the number of tokens emitted.

[14:56] Samir Khan: Do you have evidence of that? Like log fields.

[15:00] Nadia Rahman: Yes, in our usage export there are fields like prompt_tokens, completion_tokens, billed_tokens, and flags for streaming and cache hits.

[15:12] Elena Petrova: Can we get that schema ahead of time?

[15:14] Jordan Blake: Yes.

[15:16] Priya Desai: Also your data retention: how long do you retain usage logs?

[15:22] Nadia Rahman: Usage and billing records are retained for audit and finance reasons; detailed request logs may have shorter retention. We can provide retention ranges; for some plans we can extend.

[15:35] Samir Khan: We’ll need minimum. Our policy says 13 months for billing evidence.

[15:40] Sofia Mendes: We can align on that for usage/billing records.

[15:44] Mark Liu: Another redline: “Redwood may modify the measurement methods.” We want: “No change that materially increases fees without 30 days notice and the right to terminate.”

[15:56] Jordan Blake: We can do notice for material changes.

[15:59] Sofia Mendes: The termination right we can discuss—usually if it’s a material adverse change. We can propose standard language.

[16:07] Priya Desai: We want that.

[16:09] Jordan Blake: Okay.

[16:10] Mark Liu: Are you ISO or SOC 2? (Sorry, side question.)

[16:14] Jordan Blake: SOC 2 Type II.

[16:16] Samir Khan: For audit logs we might ask for a SOC report excerpt.

[16:20] Jordan Blake: We can provide under NDA.

[16:22] Nadia Rahman: Just to bring it back to usage—there’s also a “usage freeze” at month end on our side to stabilize invoicing. During the freeze, late events get handled in a controlled way.

[16:34] Elena Petrova: That’s good to know. Does that mean the usage API changes after the freeze?

[16:40] Nadia Rahman: The usage API is near-real-time; for invoicing, we cut off at a defined time. If there are late events, they get evaluated and typically applied forward, not as silent retro changes. But we should document it.

[16:56] Mark Liu: Yes, document it.

[16:58] Priya Desai: We need it in plain language.

[17:02] Jordan Blake: Yep.

[17:03] Mark Liu: Let’s talk about invoice disputes process. We want: notice, investigation, and no collection activity while dispute is pending.

[17:12] Sofia Mendes: We can add a standard “good faith dispute” clause: undisputed amounts remain payable; disputed amounts paused; both parties cooperate. Typical.

[17:24] Priya Desai: Great.

[17:25] Elena Petrova: Also we want ability to export by model and region because pricing might differ.

[17:31] Nadia Rahman: Yes, region and model are dimensions in usage events. We fixed some region attribution issues recently, but going forward it’s standard.

[17:40] Elena Petrova: Okay.

[17:41] Mark Liu: Can we restrict processing to US regions only?

[17:45] Jordan Blake: For Hosted API, we can pin region; for some fallbacks we may route within the same geo unless you disallow. For private/dedicated we can fully control.

[17:58] Samir Khan: We will likely require US-only, no cross-region fallback without approval.

[18:03] Nadia Rahman: We can configure routing policy accordingly.

[18:07] Mark Liu: Back to usage. If you do fallback to another model, do you charge at the original model rate or the fallback rate?

[18:17] Jordan Blake: Good question.

[18:18] Nadia Rahman: In general, billing is tied to the model actually served, because costs differ. But we can set policies: if fallback is triggered by Redwood capacity issues, we may bill at the contracted model rate or provide credits. That’s something we can capture in the order form as a “fallback billing policy.”

[18:41] Mark Liu: We need that spelled out. Otherwise you can route us to something more expensive.

[18:46] Jordan Blake: Completely agree. For enterprise, we don’t do surprise expensive fallbacks.

[18:52] Sofia Mendes: We can add: “No substitutions that materially increase fees without Customer consent,” and/or “fallbacks will be billed no higher than the primary model rate when fallback is due to Redwood service issues.”

[19:07] Priya Desai: Yes.

[19:09] Elena Petrova: And those fallbacks should show in the usage export.

[19:12] Nadia Rahman: They do; model_id is captured per request.

[19:16] Samir Khan: On audit logs, also want to know: can Redwood support SSO for the console so that access is controlled?

[19:23] Jordan Blake: Yes, SAML/SSO.

[19:24] Sofia Mendes: That’s typically in the security exhibit.

[19:27] Mark Liu: Okay.

[19:29] (crosstalk)

[19:30] Priya Desai: Sorry, one more: your limitation of liability excludes “billing errors.” We want billing errors carved out at least for reimbursement.

[19:40] Sofia Mendes: We typically don’t carve out billing errors entirely, but we do commit to correcting them. Liability carve-outs are a bigger conversation. We can propose a remedy framework: correction/credit is the primary remedy for billing disputes.

[19:56] Mark Liu: That may be fine if it’s clear and timely.

[20:00] Jordan Blake: We can be pragmatic there.

[20:03] Priya Desai: Okay.

[20:05] Mark Liu: Can you explain “billed tokens vs raw tokens” again, just at a high level we can put in our internal doc.

[20:12] Nadia Rahman: Sure. Raw tokens are the literal tokens in the input and output based on the model tokenizer. Billed tokens are the tokens that count for invoicing after applying billing rules: dedupe/idempotency, cache-hit adjustments, and certain error handling. We aim for billed tokens to reflect the fair, non-duplicative usage.

[20:37] Mark Liu: So billed tokens can be less than raw.

[20:40] Nadia Rahman: Yes.

[20:41] Elena Petrova: Can it be more?

[20:44] Nadia Rahman: It should not be more. If it is, that’s a bug.

[20:47] Jordan Blake: And we’d fix/credit.

[20:49] Mark Liu: Put that in writing.

[20:51] Sofia Mendes: We can add a principle statement: billed usage will not exceed metered raw usage for the same requests, except as expressly stated. We’ll be careful with wording.

[21:06] Priya Desai: Great.

[21:08] Samir Khan: What about embeddings? We may use embeddings and chat.

[21:12] Nadia Rahman: Embeddings are billed per input tokens (or per 1K tokens). For batched requests, we sum tokens across inputs. It’s included in the usage export as a separate route type.

[21:25] Elena Petrova: For batches, do you count overhead? Like separators.

[21:28] Nadia Rahman: It’s tokenization of the actual inputs; any separators included in the serialized format would count, but the SDK is consistent. We can provide examples.

[21:41] Mark Liu: Okay.

[21:43] Priya Desai: Let’s talk timeline. We want to wrap redlines this month.

[21:49] Jordan Blake: We can. Sofia can send revised clause options by Friday.

[21:54] Sofia Mendes: Yep, by end of day Friday.

[21:56] Mark Liu: Include a version that uses our template structure, if possible.

[22:01] Sofia Mendes: I’ll map it to your template sections.

[22:04] Jordan Blake: Anything else you want to cover today?

[22:07] Elena Petrova: Just confirm: we can get a daily export, in UTC, with model, region, billed tokens, raw tokens, cache hit flag, and request id?

[22:18] Nadia Rahman: Request id might be too granular for daily export depending on volume, but we can include it in API-level retrieval or provide a hashed id. Aggregated daily export will have the dimensions. We’ll confirm.

[22:34] Elena Petrova: Aggregated is okay, but for disputes we need drill-down capability.

[22:40] Jordan Blake: We’ll make sure you can drill down.

[22:42] Samir Khan: For audit logs, we need at least admin access logs and retention. Evidence on request.

[22:50] Sofia Mendes: Noted.

[22:52] Mark Liu: And dispute window: we’re proposing 60 days, with invoice preview.

[22:57] Jordan Blake: We’ll come back with a proposal: 3-business-day preview + 45 or 60 day dispute window, and a good-faith dispute process.

[23:08] Priya Desai: Great.

[23:10] Jordan Blake: Okay, I’m going to recap next steps, then we can end early if nothing else.

[23:16] Jordan Blake: Sofia will send updated usage definition clause options—token definition, retries, caching, fallbacks, dispute language—by Friday. Nadia will send a metering semantics one-pager, including streaming and billed vs raw tokens and cache hit flags, plus schema pointers. We’ll propose invoice preview workflow. And then we’ll schedule a follow-up redline working session next week.

[23:40] Priya Desai: Sounds good.

[23:41] Mark Liu: Yep.

[23:42] Samir Khan: Thanks.

[23:43] Elena Petrova: Thanks.

[23:45] Jordan Blake: Great. Ending recording.

---

Note: Transcript ends early due to participants dropping; recording shows 52 minutes total including pre-join/hold and post-call idle time. Primary discussion content occurred in the first ~24 minutes.
